source_refs.note: Chladni Plate: a main subheading of 14.11 Sharpness of Resonance, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 40-40.

blocks.text: A Chladni plate is a good example of resonance and it demonstrates a standing waves pattern. It is usually a circular or square shaped metal plate which is fixed horizontally to a vibrator and is driven transversally at its centre as shown in Fig. (14.20). When the plate is vibrated at the frequency of a resonant normal mode, the nodes and antinodes are formed over the surface of the plate.

blocks.alt: (a) Classical Chladni plate: a flat square plate on a central support, held at one edge and bowed with a violin bow at the other while sand falls from a sand shaker; the sand lies along a grid of nodal lines. (b) Modern Chladni plate: the flat plate sits on a mechanical oscillator fed by an electrical signal input, with sand from a shaker forming rings.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.22: Chladni plates, (a) classical and (b) modern (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.22).

blocks.text: The metal plate does not vibrate at points where nodes are formed while the rest of the plate is vibrating with its maximum amplitude. In order to observe such pattern, sand is sprinkled evenly in the form of a thin layer over the plate. Hence, the sand will vibrate and shift from antinode to nodes because the nodes are stationary.
